 Officials Say They Did A ‘Real Good Job’ On Election Day — But Alders Rip Ballot Shortages, Long Waits 
 Alderpeople criticized the Chicago Board of Elections Monday over ballot shortages, long lines and other issues during last week’s election. 
 by 
 Kade Heather 
 2 hours ago November 9, 2026

 People wait in line for roughly two hours at 3:30 p.m. to vote at the Downtown supersite voting location at 137 S. State St. on Election Day on Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Colin Boyle/Block Club Chicago 
 CITY HALL — Chicago Board of Elections leaders defended its handling of last week’s election as alderpeople pressed them Monday over ballot shortages, long lines and other problems that frustrated voters across the city.
 A coding error caused 24 of the city’s 1,291 precincts to run short of certain ballot styles during the Nov. 3 election, Board of Elections Executive Director Sandra Aspera told the City Council’s Budget and Government Operations Committee. 
 Officials said the city had printed enough ballots overall, but the error misallocated different ballot styles at precincts where voters received different ballots depending on their addresses. The error caused some locations to receive too few of certain styles and too many of others. 
 Aspera apologized to voters who encountered long lines in polling places across the city and said the board has added safeguards to prevent the problem from happening again.
 “Under my watch, this will not happen again,” Aspera said.
 When Ald. Bill Conway (34th) asked whether election officials thought they did a good job on Election Day, Aspera said she felt the board’s staff “did a real good job.” 
 Conway said he was “wildly concerned” that she thought they had done well, adding that his constituents were “very frustrated.”
 Aspera said the ballot error “created a lot of media attention,” but said there were “many” reasons for long lines, including what she described as a high turnout, considerable same-day registration and a shortage of voting machines at busy sites. The final turnout was about 45 percent, which was about the same as the 2022 midterms.
 Conway said his ward experienced numerous problems on Election Day, including a malfunctioning ballot feeder and delays getting replacement ballots to a polling location. He said he called the board of elections twice after being told more ballots were on the way, but they never arrived; officials instead sent an additional voting machine.
 At one site near the University of Illinois Chicago, Conway said, students waited more than three and a half hours to vote. 
 People wait in line for roughly two hours at 3:30 p.m. to vote at the Downtown supersite voting location at 137 S. State St. on Election Day on Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Colin Boyle/Block Club Chicago 
 Ald. Byron Sigcho-Lopez (25th) also criticized the board’s response to ballot shortages, saying replacement ballots did not arrive quickly enough and some residents left lines without casting ballots.
 “We lost people’s ability to vote and that is just unacceptable,” Sigcho-Lopez said. “I don’t think we can characterize this as a good job.”
 Sigcho-Lopez also questioned how the board could run short of basic supplies like pens and clipboards, and said the problems reflected poor preparation for an election which officials should have expected to draw a heavy turnout. 
 Board of Elections general counsel Adam Lasker said the board began printing replacement ballots after identifying the affected precincts. But printing 100 ballots takes about 45 minutes, Aspera said, and the ballots then had to be delivered from a warehouse. She described one location in Sigcho-Lopez’s ward where replacement ballots were delivered after 7 p.m.
 Lasker said the board had an emergency plan for ballot shortages, but its in-house printers are not designed for high-volume printing. The board is discussing whether to add more printers. 
 Election officials said the board had printed more than enough ballots overall: 10% more than the number of registered voters in each precinct. Its information technology department has since added automated checks to catch errors before ballot quantities are sent to the print vendor. Aspera said she is also requiring approvals throughout the ballot-making and printing process.
 Lasker said some supersites had about 80 voting machines and roughly 500 people waiting, arguing that the bottleneck was the number of machines available rather than the check-in process or missing ballots.
 Conway questioned whether the board could do more to prevent such delays, especially as officials plan to use the same voting equipment for the 2027 municipal election and the 2028 presidential election. The city’s contract for its current voting equipment ends in November 2028.
 Several alderpeople also raised concerns about communication with the board, saying they struggled to find the right people to contact when problems arose at polling places. Several said the board’s general phone line was not useful when they needed immediate help on Election Day.
 A few other alderpeople also raised concerns about a temporary poll book error that showed some voters as having already voted when they had not. Election officials said the issue lasted only a few minutes.
 Monday’s hearing came as the election board seeks a $48.5 million budget for 2027, an increase of about $20.6 million from this year. The increase is largely tied to preparations for next year’s municipal election and the 2028 presidential election.
 Board officials also discussed potentially adapting a ballot-on-demand system for future elections. The system would allow ballots to be printed at polling places, eliminating the need to predict how many of each ballot style each precinct will need. It could also eventually allow voters to cast ballots at any Election Day polling place, rather than only the precinct assigned to their addresses.
 Lasker said the board is considering the system as it prepares to seek new voting equipment after 2028.
